summary.text:
Staffordshire publishes a treasury contact with an address, so it is email-ready. Our PWLB file holds 49 loans at exactly £322,000,000, all MATURITY profile, against their §22 'PWLB fixed maturity loans 322.000' — to the pound, and the profile matches the row's own name. Appendices 1 to 5 are not held, so there is no CFR and no prudential indicator, and we assert nothing about the balance sheet.

The lead is paragraph 10: the twelfth LOBO call in our file. The lender exercised its call options and raised the rate, and Staffordshire repaid the £15.000m early rather than accept. Twelve calls across nine councils now, and every one refused or repaid. £18m of LOBOs remain. The £15.000m plus a £15.500m maturity is exactly the £30.500m of repayments in the cash table, which itself foots and from which all three derived figures in §10 rebuild.

Second, paragraph 51 is the best investment disclosure we have read this year and the only one naming every local authority counterparty. Lending to other councils went from £30.000m to £152.000m in twelve months, spread across twenty-five authorities at £5m or less each. Three of them we already hold from the borrowing side: Cornwall, which paid 8.50% for four days over this year end; Harlow, 7.75% for a month; and Central Bedfordshire, which borrowed £10m from Enfield at 6.50%. The whole appendix reconciles to the credit-rating table in both directions.

Third, §49 is unusually candid. The £30m of long-term local authority investments made in 2013 at 4.02% were well above the market then and performed for a decade; the table two paragraphs earlier now shows the portfolio at 4.29% with them in and 4.31% with them out. The trade has crossed from best-in-portfolio to a two-basis-point drag and the report says so while claiming the credit. On today's repayment curve the book carries about £27.4m of net discount, and their §24(c) is exactly right that the premium sits on the expensive legacy debt.

officer.reconciliation: 49 loans, exactly £322,000,000, all MATURITY, against their §22 £322.000m of PWLB fixed maturity loans. §22 foots (322.000 + 18.000 + 183.829 = 523.829; 322 + 18 = £340m). §9 cash table foots (169.878 + 2.705 − 19.254 + 30.500 = 183.829) and all three §10 derived figures rebuild (16.549, 13.951, 30.500). §51 reconciles to §38 in both directions: LA 30.000 + 122.000 = 152.000; MMFs 163.495 + 20.000 = 183.495 AAA; bond funds 75.000; banks 45.425 splitting 15.425 AA / 30.000 A; total 455.920. Prior year column foots to 422.712. §48 differentials 4.87−4.28 = 0.59 and 4.29−3.52 = 0.77. NO CFR AND NO BALANCE SHEET IDENTITY — Appendix 3 not held, and nothing is asserted about it.
officer.body:
Hi Justin,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Cabinet on 15 July and Corporate Overview and Scrutiny on 28 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, with one thing we could not do. We hold 49 PWLB loans for Staffordshire totalling exactly £322,000,000, all of them maturity profile, against the £322.000m of "PWLB fixed maturity loans" in your paragraph 22 — to the pound, and the profile matches the name of the row. Paragraph 22 foots, the cash table at paragraph 9 foots, and all three derived figures in paragraph 10 rebuild from it: £19.254m of MRP less £2.705m of new debt is the £16.549m you quote, £183.829m less £169.878m is the £13.951m, and the £15.500m maturity plus the £15.000m LOBO is the £30.500m of repayments. What we could not do is close the balance sheet, because Appendix 3 and the prudential indicators are not in what we hold — so nothing below rests on a CFR figure.

We wrote because of paragraph 10.

Your lender exercised its call options, asked for a higher rate, and you repaid the £15.000m early instead. That is the twelfth LOBO call we have picked up across the sector since the spring, across nine councils now, and every single one has gone the same way: the borrower declined and the loan was repaid or refinanced. Not one authority in our file has accepted an increase.

That is worth knowing with £18m still outstanding. A LOBO's lender option only has value if the borrower accepts, and a sector-wide refusal record of twelve out of twelve says the option is currently worth very little — which is presumably why lenders are exercising at all, and why the answer has been the same everywhere. If another call arrives, the pattern is a useful thing to have in front of the Panel.

Second, paragraph 51. It is the best investment disclosure we have read this year, and the only one anywhere that names every local authority counterparty. We checked it: it reconciles to your credit-rating table in both directions and totals £455.920m to the thousand pounds.

What it shows is a fivefold move. Lending to other councils went from £30.000m to £152.000m in twelve months, across twenty-five authorities at £5m or less each, and paragraph 40 says plainly why — the rates on offer. We can put your side of that in context, because we track the market from both ends. Three of the names on your list appear in our file as borrowers this year at rates that will interest you: Cornwall, which paid Blackburn with Darwen 8.50% for four days over this year end; Harlow, which paid 7.75% for a month; and Central Bedfordshire, which borrowed £10m from Enfield at 6.50% for thirty days. At the other end, Gloucestershire borrowed £55m at 4.15% to 4.70% in the same winter. That is a four hundred basis point range in one market in one year, and no council can see its shape from its own trades. It is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, alongside the monthly PWLB picture — July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%.

Third, and this is a compliment rather than a point. Paragraph 49 records that the £30m of long-term local authority investments made in 2013 at 4.02% were well above the market at the time and performed for a decade. Your own table two paragraphs earlier then shows the portfolio returning 4.29% with them included and 4.31% without. So the trade has crossed over — from the best thing in the portfolio to a two-basis-point drag — and the report states both facts in the same breath. Very few annual reports show the adjustment that undercuts the claim they have just made. It is the reason we can take the rest of the document at face value.

One last note, on your paragraph 24(c) — that a margin on early repayment meant the portfolio attracted a premium on the more expensive debt. On the DMO's curve this afternoon that is exactly right, and we can size both halves: the 14 loans above par carry £11.1m of premium and are the legacy coupons, including £5m at 8.38% to 2054 and £5m at 7.88% to 2055; the other 35 carry £38.5m of discount, for about £27.4m net. We're not suggesting anything follows. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. The reason it is worth a line is that the split moves with the curve, and yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Staffordshire. Alternatives to PWLB covers LOBOs and the sector's call record. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to the £152m and the twenty-five counterparties. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator sizes 24(c). All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
